newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fashion upstarts give veterans run for money.
newsitem.headline: Fashion upstarts give veterans run for money.

text.p: The emergence of four dynamic young talents on the couture circuit at this week's spring-summer shows gave the more established Paris names a run for their money, driving them to a competitive game of one-upmanship.
"It was a very eclectic season but I love the electricity in Paris this week. It's breathed new life into couture," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue.

Alexander McQueen's debut at Givenchy, John Galliano's for its sister house Christian Dior and the first adventures into couture by high-profile ready-to-wear designers Thierry Mugler and Jean-Paul Gaultier were the season's high points.
They created an almost hysterical sense of anticipation and pushed the stakes higher than they have been in many years, possibly decades.
The result was a battle between young and old, classic and modern, French and foreign.
"It's always good to add new blood. It fires everyone up and they make an extra effort," said Joan Kaner of Neiman Marcus.

Galliano won widespread acclaim for breathing fresh exuberance into Dior while keeping in touch with the label's spirit. However McQueen's collection in white and gold remained controversial -- even the exquisitely styled Botticelli and Maria Callas gowns were hard to see amid a clutter of antiquity-inspired paraphernalia.
"I wish he'd give up some of the fun and games. Everyone knows he can cut, he just has to let that show," Kaner said.
"That doesn't bother me," said Fischelis. "I thought McQueen deserved much more from the press. It was extremely coherent. He showed us he can do wonderful things with soft fabrics."
Meanwhile, the pressure compelled veterans like Yves Saint Laurent and Karl Lagerfeld for Chanel to push the classics to new heights of elegance.
Didier Grumbach, chairman of Thierry Mugler, felt the budding talent was part of couture's healthy and quite normal evolution.

"The arrival of new talent is not a novelty. In 1962 the avant-gardists were Saint Laurent, Philippe Venet, Andre Courreges and Jean-Louis Scherrer," he said. "There have always been foreigners in Paris. Take Balenciaga and Schiaparelli."
Cristobal Balenciaga, a Spaniard, and Elsa Shiaparelli, an Italian, were both pioneering designers who opened their fashion houses between the two world wars.
This season at least one of the more traditional haute couture houses felt threatened by the new upstarts.
The Jean-Louis Scherrer fashion house staged its own private showing after the official season had ended, angry at Mugler and Gaultier's participation.
